strengths: Clear and well-motivated diagnosis of two distinct failure modes (count failures and semantic mixing) in multi-instance T2I generation, supported by an insightful analysis (Fig. 2/3) showing that self-attention encodes instance structure earlier than cross-attention encodes reliable semantics.

The proposed two-phase hierarchical formulation (instance formation via self-attention clustering + repel loss, then instance-aware semantic separation via a repel-and-bind cross-attention loss) is a sensible, well-motivated design that explicitly targets the diagnosed failure modes rather than only manipulating semantic signals as prior training-free methods do.

Extensive empirical validation: results are reported across many diffusion backbones (SD1.4/1.5/2.1, SDXL, SD3.5-M/L, PixArt-α/Σ, Flux.1-dev, Qwen-Image) and across three benchmarks (T2I-CompBench, HRS-Bench, and the newly introduced IntraCompBench), consistently showing gains over multiple training-free and count-supervised baselines.

Thorough ablations: loss schedule ordering (Table 5), similarity metric choice (MPO vs MAE/KL/IoU, Table 6), clustering algorithm choice (Table 7), step-size sensitivity (Fig. 8), and layer-wise cost/quality trade-off (Table 14) are all examined.

Good breadth of applicability: the method is shown to help layout-to-image controllers (GLIGEN + CAR&SAR), fine-tuned models (TokenCompose, IterComp), and is complemented by a gradient-free "latent selection" variant (ISAC_LS) for scalability to very large models, plus image-quality trade-off is quantified via FID/CMMD.

IntraCompBench addresses a genuine gap in existing benchmarks by isolating intra-category multi-object composition, which is argued (and shown qualitatively/quantitatively) to be a harder and previously under-tested regime.

Reasonable transparency about limitations (3D/occlusion reasoning failure mode, ambiguous count expressions, VRAM/latency overhead) and detailed appendix on implementation and prompt-parsing procedure supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core building blocks (self-attention-based clustering for instance masks, repel/bind losses on cross-attention) are individually adaptations of ideas already present in InitNO, Self-Cross, SynGen, and CONFORM; the main novelty is the explicit two-phase, instance-first sequencing and scheduling, which is a comparatively incremental algorithmic contribution though reasonably well executed.

The method still requires instance counts and class/attribute relations extracted via an LLM parser; while this avoids fine-tuning, it is a form of supervision at inference time, and parsing errors (e.g., ambiguous quantifiers like "a few", "several") are acknowledged but not resolved, which could affect real-world robustness beyond the curated benchmarks.

Automatic evaluation relies entirely on an ensemble of open-vocabulary detectors (Grounding DINO, YOLOE, YOLOv12) with a 2-of-3 agreement rule; no human evaluation is provided to validate that this proxy faithfully captures perceptual count/semantic correctness, and detector biases could systematically favor or disfavor certain methods.

Latent optimization increases VRAM/latency by 2–3x over baselines (further exacerbated for large models), and the proposed gradient-free alternative (ISAC_LS) requires best-of-10 sampling, which itself multiplies compute cost substantially; the practical efficiency trade-offs for large-scale deployment remain non-trivial.

IntraCompBench is restricted to a subset of COCO's 80 classes (explicitly excluding e.g. "person", ambiguous/small objects), which limits the diversity and generality of the new benchmark's claims relative to open-world compositional scenarios.

Most quantitative comparisons are reported as single-run averages without confidence intervals or statistical significance testing (aside from the seed-stability analysis in Appendix C.4 on a narrower subset), making it harder to assess how robust the reported margins are, especially for smaller benchmarks/settings.

strengths: The core diagnosis—that self-attention reveals instance structure earlier and more reliably than cross-attention, and that prior training-free methods conflate instance separation with semantic separation—is well motivated and supported by a clear empirical analysis (Fig. 2, Fig. 3).

The two-phase (instance-first, then semantic) formulation is a clean, interpretable idea, and the loss design (MPO-based repel/bind objectives, instance-to-semantic scheduling) is reasonably simple to implement without any fine-tuning.

The experimental scope is unusually broad for a training-free method: five diffusion backbones, T2I-CompBench, HRS-Bench, the authors' new IntraCompBench, layout-to-image (GLIGEN) settings, latent-selection and fine-tuned-model variants, FID/CMMD quality checks, seed-stability analysis, and multiple ablations (loss schedule, similarity metric, clustering algorithm, layer selection).

Consistent, often large, quantitative gains over strong recent training-free baselines (InitNO, Self-Cross, A&E, SynGen, CONFORM, TEBOpt) and even over count-supervised methods (CountGen, Counting Guidance) despite using no auxiliary training, which is a meaningful practical result.

Good transparency about limitations (3D/occlusion failure case, VRAM/latency overhead, ambiguous count parsing, incompatibility with public OverlayBench annotations), and reasonably detailed reproducibility information (prompt-parsing prompts, hyperparameter sensitivity, clustering choice).
weaknesses: ISAC is not purely training-free/unsupervised in the sense of not requiring extra information at inference: it needs per-prompt instance counts and token relations extracted by an external LLM parser (GPT-OSS-20B). This is a nontrivial dependency and a form of test-time supervision that is somewhat understated relative to the 'training-free' framing; failure of the parser (e.g., on ambiguous counts like 'a few') directly propagates to generation errors, and this is only partially acknowledged.

Significant computational overhead: 2–4x VRAM and roughly 2–3x latency versus baselines (e.g., Table 2: 21s/9.7GB vs 8s/4.9GB for SD1.5; even larger multipliers for SD3.5-M and Flux/Qwen in Appendix C), which limits practicality for larger or production models; the proposed layer-restricted mitigation (Appendix D) is left as future work rather than being evaluated as a fully integrated default.

IntraCompBench, the benchmark used to report the largest gains, is introduced by the same authors and evaluated with the same authors' detector-ensemble protocol (Grounding DINO + YOLOE + YOLOv12, 2-of-3 agreement); there is no independent/human verification of this automatic evaluation, and the benchmark's class distribution is restricted to COCO countable categories, which may not generalize to broader compositional scenarios.

The K-means clustering step in Phase 1 requires knowing N in advance and its quality/robustness under incorrect or noisy instance-count estimates is not stress-tested (e.g., how ISAC behaves when the LLM parser under/over-counts is not directly quantified, only the general limitations sentence in Appendix A.1 mentions this).

Some comparisons could be seen as slightly favorable to ISAC: e.g., latency/VRAM columns are reported but not statistically paired with quality-controlled matching (same number of function evaluations, same guidance strength search for baselines), and it is unclear whether baselines were tuned as extensively as ISAC's single hyperparameter η.

Ablation and main results tables lack confidence intervals/error bars in the primary tables (Table 2–6), aside from a limited seed-variance analysis in Appendix C.4 on a single numeracy metric; broader variance reporting across the main IntraCompBench multi-class/multi-instance metrics would strengthen the statistical case.
